title: Does Loving Someone Include Letting Them No Longer Have to Depend on You?
deck: The best help allows its own success: the other person no longer has to depend on you, but can still choose you.
body: Being needed makes us feel important.

Someone turns to you first when things are difficult, asks you before making decisions, and can face life better because you are there. Helping another person find their footing brings a deep satisfaction within a relationship.
But after helping for a long time, a question that is hard to voice can arise:
If one day they no longer need me this way, what will remain between us?
And so love sometimes preserves dependence unintentionally.

We do things for the other person that they could gradually learn to do, continue offering judgments that are no longer necessary, and emphasize the risks when they are ready to try on their own. Each act of help can be explained as care, yet together they maintain a position: without me, you cannot do it.
This does not necessarily arise from a desire to control.
We may simply fear that once we are no longer irreplaceable, the relationship will lose its reason to exist.
Yet if help can prove its value only through the other person’s continuing lack of some ability, it can hardly be truly centered on them.
Good help should be able to allow its own success.
And one sign of successful help is precisely that some things begin to no longer require the helper.

Someone can deal independently with problems that once left them confused, make judgments without approval, and bear the consequences of choices that differ from yours. This may make some aspects of the relationship less close-knit, yet add another kind of authenticity.
They no longer stay merely because they cannot leave.
Letting someone no longer have to depend on you does not mean demanding a relationship entirely free of dependence.

People entrust time, feelings, care, and resources to one another. Deep relationships naturally make both more susceptible to each other’s influence. Treating every need as immaturity only makes people afraid to truly rely on anyone.
The difference between needing and being possessed is not whether dependence exists, but whether there is a way to leave it or change it.
One kind of dependence adjusts as abilities grow. What you take on today can be handed back tomorrow; someone who gains new support will not therefore be accused of betrayal.

Another kind of dependence is fixed in place. The helper continually proves indispensable, while the person helped gradually comes to believe that acting independently means being ungrateful or no longer loving.
At this point, the relationship no longer protects the people, but their original roles.
Genuine care asks: What can I do to give them more choices in the future?

Sometimes the answer is to keep staying, sometimes to do less on their behalf, and sometimes to hand over knowledge, resources, and the process of deciding. Stepping back is no easier than reaching out, because it requires the helper to let go of a contribution whose effects are immediately visible.
After accomplishing something on their own, the person may no longer thank you in the same way.
They may choose a different path from yours, even using the abilities you taught them in a direction you do not approve of.
If help counts as successful only when its result meets the helper’s expectations, what has been developed is merely more effective obedience.
Letting them no longer have to depend on you also means acknowledging that even after gaining abilities, they are still not your creation.
Of course, stepping back cannot be an excuse for suddenly withdrawing a commitment.

Some dependencies are established together and also involve real caregiving responsibilities. Before the other person has alternatives available, you cannot suddenly say “You should be independent,” presenting your departure as a demand for growth.
Reducing dependence requires just as much responsibility as establishing it.

It should take ability, time, and transition into account, and let the other person participate in deciding. Truly handing things back does not mean pushing someone away. It means gradually returning to their hands what they can manage while support is still in place.
Loving someone sometimes does indeed include letting them no longer have to depend on you.
This does not mean making them never need anyone again. It means not treating your irreplaceability as the surest proof of the relationship’s security.
The strongest relationship is not necessarily “You cannot live without me.”
It can also be:
“You can now live by your own reasons and still want to let me into your life; I do not need your inability to confirm my own importance either.”
Being needed is one kind of intimacy.
Being able to be no longer needed, yet still chosen, is another, more difficult kind.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
